articles.title: GRE format at a glance
lines: The GRE General Test is the admissions exam many graduate and business programs ask for. Since September 2023 it has been a shorter test: about 1 hour 58 minutes from the first question to the last. Knowing exactly what is coming, in what order and for how long, removes a surprising amount of stress on test day and lets you plan your pacing in advance.
## The five parts
- Analytical Writing: one "Analyze an Issue" task, 30 minutes.
- Verbal Reasoning, section 1: 12 questions in 18 minutes.
- Verbal Reasoning, section 2: 15 questions in 23 minutes.
- Quantitative Reasoning, section 1: 12 questions in 21 minutes.
- Quantitative Reasoning, section 2: 15 questions in 26 minutes.

Analytical Writing always comes first. After it, the two Verbal sections and the two Quant sections follow, but the order can vary: you might see Verbal first or Quant first. Do not build your plan around one fixed order. Practice both, so that neither surprises you.
## What changed in 2023

If you read older books or forum posts, be careful. The older test was close to four hours long. It had two essays, longer sections, an unscored research section and a scheduled ten-minute break. The current test has one essay, shorter sections, no unscored section and no scheduled break. Advice about "the experimental section" or "using your break to eat a snack" no longer applies.
! Because there is no unscored section, every question you see counts. You never have to guess which section is "real".
## How the sections work

Each Verbal and Quant measure has two sections. The first section is the same medium mix of difficulty for everyone. Your result on it decides whether your second section is easier, medium or harder. This is called section-level adaptive testing, and it is explained in detail in the scoring article. The short version: do your very best on the first section of each measure.

Inside a section, the test behaves like a paper test. You can skip a question, mark it, go back to it later and change any answer until the section timer runs out. Once a section ends, you cannot return to it.
## Scores in one paragraph

Verbal and Quant are each scored from 130 to 170 in 1-point steps. Analytical Writing is scored from 0 to 6 in half-point steps. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so you should answer every question. Scores stay valid for five years.
## Tools on screen
- An on-screen basic calculator is available in Quant sections only. It adds, subtracts, multiplies, divides and takes square roots. It is not a scientific calculator.
- A review screen lists every question in the section and shows which ones you answered and which ones you marked.
- A timer counts down in the corner. You can hide it if it makes you nervous, but check it at regular points.
- You get material for notes: scratch paper at a test center, or a small whiteboard or approved transparent sheet at home (check the current rules on ets.org).
## Time per question at a glance
> Verbal section 1: 18 min for 12 questions = 90 seconds each on average
> Verbal section 2: 23 min for 15 questions = 92 seconds each on average
> Quant section 1: 21 min for 12 questions = 105 seconds each on average
> Quant section 2: 26 min for 15 questions = 104 seconds each on average
These are averages. Short vocabulary questions take less time; reading passages and data questions take more. The time management article gives a target for each question type.
## Where you can take it

You can take the GRE at a test center or at home on your own computer with a remote proctor. The content, timing and scoring are the same. Registration details, fees and available dates change, so always check them on ets.org.
## How this app mirrors the real test
- Every one of the 20 mock tests follows the real order and timing: essay first, then four sections of 12, 15, 12 and 15 questions.
- Section 2 of each measure adapts to your section 1 result, as on the real test.
- Each mock gives estimated Verbal and Quant scores on the 130-170 scale, and every answer is explained.
- After the essay, you rate yourself against a model essay using the 0-6 scale.
Start with one mock test early, even before you feel ready. It shows you the format in action, gives you a baseline score and tells the Progress tab which topics to put first.

articles.title: A tour of every question type
lines: The GRE uses a small set of question formats again and again. Once you know each format, you stop spending time working out what a question wants and can spend it on the actual thinking. Here is every type, with a tiny original example of each. The examples are easy on purpose; real items are harder, but the shape is the same.
## Verbal: Text Completion

A short passage of one to five sentences with one, two or three blanks. One-blank items have five choices; two- and three-blank items have three choices per blank. You must get every blank right to earn the point. There is no partial credit.
> Although the new bridge looked fragile, engineers insisted it was remarkably _____.
> (A) ornate (B) sturdy (C) costly (D) temporary (E) narrow
> Answer: (B) sturdy. "Although" signals a contrast with "fragile".
! Read the whole passage before looking at the choices, and predict your own word for each blank.
## Verbal: Sentence Equivalence
One sentence, one blank, six choices. You pick exactly two choices that both fit and give sentences with nearly the same meaning. Both must be right to earn credit.
> The professor was known for her _____ lectures, which rarely ran past twenty minutes.
> (A) brief (B) lively (C) concise (D) dense (E) famous (F) technical
> Answer: (A) brief and (C) concise.
! Two words that are synonyms of each other are not automatically correct; they must also fit the sentence.
## Verbal: Reading Comprehension
Passages range from one paragraph to several. Questions come in three formats.
- Multiple choice, one answer: five choices, pick one.
- Multiple choice, select one or more: three choices, pick every correct one (one, two or all three). No partial credit.
- Select in passage: click the sentence in the passage that does what the question describes.
> Passage: Honeybees communicate the location of food through a "waggle dance". The angle of the dance shows direction relative to the sun, and its length shows distance.
> Question (select one or more): Which of the following does the dance convey? (A) direction (B) distance (C) type of flower
> Answer: (A) and (B). The passage never mentions flower type.
Some short passages are arguments, followed by one question asking what would strengthen, weaken or support the argument, or what assumption it relies on.
## Quant: Quantitative Comparison
You compare Quantity A with Quantity B and choose one of four fixed options: A is greater, B is greater, the two are equal, or the relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
> x is a number with x² = 9
> Quantity A: x    Quantity B: 2
> Answer: cannot be determined. x could be 3 (A greater) or −3 (B greater).
! If you find two allowed cases that give different results, the answer is "cannot be determined". Always test negatives, zero and fractions.
## Quant: Multiple Choice, one answer
A question with five choices; one is right.
> If 3n + 4 = 19, what is n?
> Answer: (C) 5.
## Quant: Multiple Choice, one or more answers
Several choices (often three to eight). The question may say "Indicate all such values". You must pick every correct choice and no wrong one.
> Which of the following are factors of 12? Indicate all that apply.
> Answer: (A) and (C).
## Quant: Numeric Entry

No choices: you type the answer into a box. Some items have two boxes for a fraction (numerator and denominator). Fractions do not need to be reduced unless asked; decimals must follow any rounding instruction.
> A shirt costs $40 and is discounted by 15%. What is the sale price, in dollars?
> Answer: 34
! With no choices to check against, reread the question to confirm the units and what exactly is being asked before you type.
## Quant: Data Interpretation

A set of two or three questions shares one table or chart. The questions themselves are multiple choice or numeric entry. Most need you to read two values, find a percent change, compare ratios or make a quick estimate.
> A chart shows a company's sales: 200 units in 2021 and 250 in 2022.
> Question: By what percent did sales increase? Answer: 50 ÷ 200 = 25%.
! Read the title, axis labels and units before the first question. Many traps come from reading thousands as units or a percent as a count.
## Analytical Writing: Analyze an Issue

You get a short statement on a general topic and instructions telling you how to respond, for example by discussing when the statement would and would not hold. You have 30 minutes to plan and type an essay that takes a clear position and supports it with reasons and examples. The essay article in Strategy gives a template.
## How to practice the types in this app
Every Verbal and Quant topic in the app has its own lesson and practice set, so you can drill one format until it feels routine. Then use the mock tests, where the types are mixed as on test day.

articles.title: How scoring and the adaptive sections work
lines: Understanding how the GRE turns your answers into a score changes how you should take the test. The most important idea is simple: in each measure, the first section decides how high your score can go.
## The three scores
- Verbal Reasoning: 130 to 170, in 1-point steps.
- Quantitative Reasoning: 130 to 170, in 1-point steps.
- Analytical Writing: 0 to 6, in half-point steps.

Verbal and Quant are reported separately; there is no official combined score, although people often add the two and talk about "a 320". Each graduate program decides how to use the scores, so check what your target programs say.
## Section-level adaptive testing
The GRE does not change difficulty after every question. Instead, it adapts between sections.
- Section 1 of Verbal (and of Quant) is a medium mix of easy, medium and hard questions. Everyone gets a similar mix.
- When section 1 ends, the test looks at how many questions you got right.
- It then gives you a section 2 that is easier, medium or harder, depending on that result.

Your final score depends on two things: how many questions you answered correctly in total, and how difficult your section 2 was. A correct answer in a harder second section is worth more than a correct answer in an easier one.
## Why section 1 matters most
Imagine two test takers, Amara and Mateo, who each answer 20 of the 27 Quant questions correctly.
> Amara gets 10 of 12 right in section 1 and receives the harder section 2, where she gets 10 of 15 right.
> Mateo gets 6 of 12 right in section 1 and receives the easier section 2, where he gets 14 of 15 right.
> Both have 20 correct answers, but Amara's score will be clearly higher, because her section 2 was harder.

This is why section 1 deserves your sharpest focus. A careless slip there can send you to an easier second section, and then even a perfect section 2 cannot lift you to the top of the scale. It is like a ceiling: section 1 sets how high the ceiling is; section 2 decides how close to it you get.
! Treat section 1 as the most important 18 or 21 minutes of the measure. Check your work, avoid silly errors and do not rush through easy questions to "save time" for later.
## What section 2 tells you

You cannot see the exact difficulty of your section 2, and you should not try to guess it during the test. A section that feels hard might mean you did well on section 1, or it might just be a hard topic for you. Either way, the right response is the same: keep working steadily, answer everything and move on from questions that take too long.
## No penalty for wrong answers

Your score counts right answers only. A wrong answer and a blank answer both count as not correct. So never leave a question unanswered. If time is running out, enter a guess on every remaining question before the timer ends.
## How the essay is scored

Your Issue essay receives a holistic score from 0 to 6. It is scored once by a trained human reader and once by a computer scoring program. If the two scores are close, they are averaged; if they disagree by too much, another human reader decides. Scores are reported in half-point steps.
- A 6 essay presents a clear, insightful position, develops it with compelling reasons and well-chosen examples, is well organized and uses language fluently and precisely, with only minor errors.
- A 4 essay has a clear position and relevant support, is adequately organized and shows reasonable control of language, with some errors.
- A 2 essay is seriously flawed: unclear position, little relevant support, poor organization or errors that often get in the way of meaning.
- A 0 is given for an essay that is off topic, not in English, copied from the prompt or empty.

Length alone does not earn points, but a strong essay usually needs enough space to develop two or three reasons properly. As a practical target, aim for roughly 400-600 words that you have time to plan and proofread.
## When do scores arrive?

Unofficial Verbal and Quant scores are shown on screen at the end of the test. Official scores, including Analytical Writing, are released later through your ETS account. Check ets.org for current timing.
## How the app estimates your score

Each mock test in this app uses the same two-stage design: your section 1 result picks an easier, medium or harder section 2. The app then estimates your Verbal and Quant scores on the 130-170 scale from your total correct and the level of your section 2. These estimates are a guide, not an official score, but they move in the same direction as the real thing: a stronger section 1 opens the door to a higher estimate.
- After each mock, look at your section 1 accuracy first. It is the lever with the biggest effect on your score.
- If you often land in the easier section 2, focus your next study week on the topics you missed in section 1.

articles.title: Test day: what to expect
lines: Test day is not the time for surprises. Most of what goes wrong on the day has nothing to do with knowledge: a late arrival, an ID problem, a noisy room or a computer that fails the system check. This article walks through the day for both test center and at-home candidates. Rules can change, so read the current requirements on ets.org a week before your test and again the day before.
## The week before
- Take your last full mock test four to six days before the exam, at the same time of day as your real test.
- Read the ID requirements on ets.org and check that the name on your ID matches your registration exactly, including the order of names and any middle name.
- Plan your route to the test center, or prepare your room and computer for an at-home test.
- Keep your sleep regular. Two nights of good sleep before the test matter more than one extra evening of study.
## Your ID

You will need valid, acceptable identification, usually an original government-issued photo ID such as a passport. Photocopies and expired documents are normally refused. If your ID is not accepted, you may not be allowed to test and may lose your fee. Check the exact rules for your country on ets.org well in advance; this is one of the most common, and most avoidable, problems.
## At a test center
- Arrive early: aim for at least 30 minutes before your appointment. Late arrivals may be turned away.
- Check-in usually includes showing your ID, a photo, signing a confidentiality statement and storing your belongings in a locker. Phones, watches, notes and food are not allowed in the testing room.
- Staff give you scratch paper and pencils for notes. You may be able to ask for more during the test; ask the center how it works.
- You may wear earplugs or headphones provided by the center if available, since other candidates may be taking different tests around you.
## At home
- Run the ETS system check on the exact computer, network and room you will use, a few days before and again on the day.
- Use a desktop or laptop (not a tablet), with a webcam, microphone and speaker. Close every other program.
- Choose a quiet, private room with a clear desk. A proctor will ask you to show the room with your camera.

- Note-taking at home is limited to approved materials, such as a small whiteboard with an erasable marker or a transparent sheet with an erasable marker. Paper is not allowed. Check ets.org for the current list, and erase your notes in front of the proctor at the end.
- Start the check-in process early. Connecting with the proctor and showing your room can take some time.
! Practice with the same note-taking tool you will use on test day. Writing on a small whiteboard is slower than on paper, so get used to it during your mock tests.
## During the test
The test opens with the 30-minute essay, then moves through the four Verbal and Quant sections. There is no scheduled break between sections. Plan for close to two hours of continuous focus.
- Use the restroom just before you start.
- Eat a normal meal one to two hours before the test, so you are neither hungry nor sleepy.
- Drink some water before, but not so much that you need to leave the room.
- If you must take an unscheduled break, the clock keeps running, and at-home rules are strict. Ask about the current rules in advance.
## Handling problems in the room

If something goes wrong, such as a frozen screen, a noise that will not stop or a calculator that does not respond, raise your hand at a center or contact the proctor through the chat at home. Report it right away, not after the test is over. Stay calm: a short pause to fix a problem is better than an hour of distraction.
## Mindset on the day
- Expect at least one question that seems impossible. Every test taker meets some. Mark it, guess and move on.
- Do not try to judge from section 2 whether you did well in section 1. It wastes attention.
- Between sections, take one slow breath, reset your posture and read the next section's first question fresh.
## After the test

At the end you will see your unofficial Verbal and Quant scores. Your official scores, with the essay score, arrive later. If you are unhappy with your result, do not decide anything that day. Rest, then read the article on retakes and use your score report to plan.
## Rehearse with the app

Take at least two of this app's mock tests as full rehearsals: same start time as your real test, phone away, no breaks, essay included, and the same note-taking tool. A rehearsal makes the real day feel familiar.

articles.title: Registering, retakes and sending scores
lines: This article gives you a general map of registering for the GRE, retaking it and sending scores to programs. The details, such as fees, available dates, deadlines and the exact number of free score reports, change from time to time and can differ by country. For anything specific, the official source is ets.org. Treat what follows as a checklist of questions to answer there.
## Before you register
- Make a list of the programs you plan to apply to and their application deadlines.
- Check whether each program requires the GRE, accepts it as optional, or prefers another test. Requirements vary a lot.
- Note any minimum or typical scores the programs publish, and whether they want the Analytical Writing score in particular.
- Work backward from your earliest deadline. Leave time for official scores to reach the programs, and room for a possible retake.
> Example plan: earliest deadline 1 December. Aim to test by early October, so a retake in early November is still possible if needed.
## Creating your ETS account

You register through an ETS account. Use your name exactly as it appears on the ID you will bring on test day. A mismatch between your account and your ID is a common reason candidates are turned away. Keep your login details safe: you will use the account to see scores and send reports later.
## Choosing center or home
You can take the test at a test center or at home with a remote proctor. The test content and scoring are the same. Think about:
- Where you focus better and feel calmer.
- Whether your home has a quiet private room and a reliable computer and internet connection.
- Whether you prefer working on scratch paper (center) or can adapt to the approved at-home note-taking materials.
- Travel time and available dates in your area.
## Choosing a date
- Pick a date after you have completed your study plan and at least four or five full mock tests.
- Choose a time of day when you are usually alert, and practice at that time.
- Avoid scheduling the test right after a heavy period at work or university.
- Read the current rules on rescheduling and cancellation before you book.
## Sending scores

On test day or afterward, you can choose institutions to receive your scores. ETS has a score-selection option that lets you choose which test dates to send, though the details of what is free and what costs extra should be checked on ets.org. Things to confirm:
- The correct code for each institution and, if required, the department.
- Whether a program wants all scores or lets you choose.
- How long it takes for official scores to reach institutions after your test.
Your scores remain valid for five years from the test date, so a strong score can serve future applications too.
## Retaking the test
Many people take the GRE more than once. A retake makes sense when:
- Your score is clearly below what your target programs expect.
- You know why it went wrong, for example timing, nerves or one weak topic, and you have a plan to fix it.
- You have enough time before your deadlines.
There are limits on how often you can retake within a period of time; check the current rules on ets.org before planning.
! A retake without a new plan usually produces a similar score. Before booking again, change something concrete: a new study focus, better timing or more full-length practice.
## A retake plan using this app
- Study your official score report and your last few mock results. Which measure, and which question types, cost the most points?
- Open the Progress tab and list your three weakest topics.
- Spend two to four weeks on those topics: the lesson first, then the practice set, then a second round of the set.
- Take a mock test every week, and track section 1 accuracy most closely.
- Book the retake only when your mock estimates are steadily above your previous result.
## Questions to settle on ets.org
- Current fees and any fee-reduction programs.
- ID requirements for your country.
- Rules on rescheduling, cancellation and retakes.
- How score selection and score reports work, and their costs.
- Test day rules for at-home testing, including the equipment and note-taking materials allowed.
Write the answers down in one place. Having them ready saves last-minute stress and lets you spend the final weeks on what matters: preparing for the questions.

articles.title: Time management section by section
lines: On the shorter GRE, every section is tight. Most people who run out of time do not work too slowly in general; they spend four minutes on one stubborn question and then rush the last five. Good pacing means deciding in advance how long each kind of question deserves and leaving the hard ones for later.
## The numbers
> Verbal: 18 min for 12 questions, then 23 min for 15 questions (about 90 seconds each)
> Quant: 21 min for 12 questions, then 26 min for 15 questions (about 105 seconds each)
> Essay: 30 min for one Issue task
## Target time per question type
Aim for the lower end of each range on most questions. That builds a buffer for review and for the odd hard question.
- Sentence Equivalence: 45-60 seconds.
- Text Completion, one blank: 45-60 seconds.
- Text Completion, two blanks: 75-90 seconds.
- Text Completion, three blanks: 90-120 seconds.
- Reading, short passage (one paragraph): about 2 minutes to read, then 45-75 seconds per question.
- Reading, long passage: about 3 minutes to read, then 60-75 seconds per question.
- Argument paragraph: about 90 seconds for the paragraph and its one question.
- Quantitative Comparison: 60-75 seconds.
- Quant multiple choice and numeric entry: 90-120 seconds.
- Data Interpretation: about 2 minutes per question, including a first look at the chart.
! Vocabulary questions (TC and SE) are your time bank in Verbal. Answer them briskly so that reading passages get the time they need.
## The two-pass method
Inside a section you can move freely, so use two passes.
- Pass 1: Go through every question in order. If you can answer it within its target time, answer it. If it looks long or you get stuck, choose your best guess, mark it and move on.
- Pass 2: Use the review screen to go back to marked questions, starting with the ones you felt closest to solving.
This method guarantees that you see every question, including easy ones near the end. It also means every question already has an answer, so running out of time costs you nothing extra.
## Mark and move: the 2-minute rule

Set a personal limit. In Verbal, if a question passes 2 minutes and you are not close, mark it. In Quant, use 2.5 minutes. The longer you stay on a question that is not working, the less likely you are to solve it, and the more you take from easier points later.

> Example: In Quant section 1 you reach question 6, a probability problem. After 90 seconds you have two possible methods and no answer. Pick the choice that seems most likely, mark it, and go to question 7. You return with 4 minutes left and solve it calmly.
## Checkpoints
Instead of looking at the timer after every question, check at fixed points.
- Verbal section 1 (12 questions, 18 min): about 12 minutes left after question 4, 6 minutes left after question 8.
- Verbal section 2 (15 questions, 23 min): about 15 minutes left after question 5, 8 minutes left after question 10.
- Quant section 1 (12 questions, 21 min): about 14 minutes left after question 4, 7 minutes left after question 8.
- Quant section 2 (15 questions, 26 min): about 17 minutes left after question 5, 9 minutes left after question 10.
If you are behind at a checkpoint, mark the next long question you meet instead of starting it.
## Section 1 versus section 2

Because section 1 decides the difficulty of section 2, accuracy in section 1 is worth slightly more than speed. Spend your buffer there on checking. In section 2, keep moving: the questions may be harder, and finishing matters.
## Reading passages
- Read the passage once, actively, noting the main point and the role of each paragraph in a few words.
- Do not try to memorize details. Go back to the passage for each detail question.
- If a passage is on a topic you find heavy, answer its general question first (the main idea), then decide whether the other questions are worth the time.
## Essay timing
- 3-5 minutes: read the task, choose a position and plan two or three reasons with examples.
- 20-22 minutes: write the introduction, body paragraphs and a short conclusion.
- 3-5 minutes: reread and fix errors.
## Training your pace in this app
- Do practice sets with the timer, and compare your time per question with the targets above.
- In mock tests, note any question that took more than 3 minutes. That topic needs work, or you need to practice letting go.
- After each mock, check how many questions you left for the last minute. If it was more than two, use the checkpoints next time.

articles.title: Verbal tips and tricks
lines: Verbal Reasoning rewards careful reading more than a huge vocabulary. The words matter, but the questions are designed so that the sentence or passage itself tells you what is needed. These habits help across all the Verbal types.
## Text Completion
- Cover the choices and read the whole passage first. Choices read too early pull you toward traps.
- Find the clue: a phrase that describes or explains the blank.
- Find the signal word. Same direction: "and", "because", "in fact", "indeed", a colon or semicolon. Opposite direction: "although", "but", "yet", "despite", "however", "rather than".
- Predict a simple word of your own, then match it to the choices.
- In multi-blank items, start with the blank that has the strongest clue, which is often not the first one.
- Reread the full passage with your choices in place. Every blank must fit together.
> Despite the reviewer's _____ tone, her conclusions were surprisingly generous.
> Signal: "Despite" shows contrast with "generous". Prediction: harsh. A word like "caustic" fits.
! A choice that sounds sophisticated is not more likely to be right. The answer is the word that fits the logic.
## Sentence Equivalence
- Predict the meaning of the blank before you look.
- Find all choices that match your prediction. You need exactly two that fit and make sentences with the same meaning.
- Watch for a pair of synonyms that does not fit the sentence. It is a common trap.
- Watch for a single word that fits well but has no partner among the choices. If no other choice means the same, it is not part of the answer.
- If you find only one good word, look for a second word that is close in meaning even if it is less familiar.
## Reading Comprehension
- Read for structure: What is the main point? What does each paragraph do (introduce, support, contrast, conclude)?
- Note the author's attitude. Words such as "unfortunately", "surprisingly" or "rightly" reveal it.
- Answer from the passage, not from what you know about the topic. A choice can be true in the real world and still wrong.
- Prefer moderate choices. Answers with "always", "never", "only" or "completely" are often too extreme for what the passage supports.
- For "select one or more" questions, judge each choice on its own. Any number from one to three can be correct.
- For select-in-passage questions, read the question carefully and test the sentences in the named part of the passage one by one.
> Typical wrong answers: too extreme, out of scope, the reverse of what is stated, true but not relevant to the question, or half right and half wrong.
! If two choices both seem right, find the single word in one of them that the passage does not support. That word makes it wrong.
## Argument paragraphs
- Find the conclusion first, then the evidence for it.
- Look for the gap between evidence and conclusion. Assumption, strengthen and weaken questions are all about that gap.
- To weaken, look for another explanation of the evidence. To strengthen, rule one out.
- For boldface questions, label each bold part: conclusion, evidence, an opposing view, or a fact the author explains.
## Building vocabulary that pays
- Learn words in context, with a sentence, not as isolated lists. The flashcards in this app each come with an example sentence and synonyms.
- Group words by meaning: words for praise, for criticism, for "changing a lot", for "stubborn". Synonym groups are exactly what Sentence Equivalence tests.
- Study a little every day. Fifteen minutes of flashcards daily beats two hours once a week.
- Learn second meanings of common words. On the GRE, "qualify" can mean "limit", "check" can mean "restrain" and "temper" can mean "moderate".
- Learn common roots: "bene-" good, "mal-" bad, "-loqu-" speak, "chron-" time. They help you guess unfamiliar words.
## When you do not know a word
- Decide whether it feels positive or negative from its roots or from words it resembles.
- Eliminate choices you know are wrong, then guess among the rest.
- Never leave a question blank, and do not spend long on a question that depends on one unknown word.
## Practice plan in the app
- Each Verbal topic has a lesson and a practice set. Do the lesson once, then do the set, then read every explanation, including for questions you got right.
- Keep a list of words you missed and add them to your flashcard review.
- In mocks, check whether your Verbal errors come from vocabulary, from reading or from timing. Each needs a different fix.

articles.title: Quant tips and tricks
lines: GRE Quant uses high-school mathematics, but it tests it in ways that reward clear thinking over long calculations. Many questions have a fast route and a slow route. These strategies help you find the fast one.
## Plugging in numbers
When a question uses variables in the choices, or says "for any positive integer n", choose simple numbers for the variables, work out the answer, and test each choice.
> If x is a positive number, which of the following equals 20% of 30% of x?
> Pick x = 100. 30% of 100 is 30, and 20% of 30 is 6. The choice that gives 6 when x = 100 is 0.06x.
- Pick numbers that are easy to work with: 2, 3, 10 or 100 for percents.
- Avoid 0 and 1 when testing choices, because many different expressions give the same result for them.
- If two choices both work, try a second number to separate them.
## Back-solving
When the choices are numbers and the question asks for one value, try the choices in the equation instead of solving it.
> A number is tripled and then increased by 7, giving 40. What is the number?
- Start with the middle choice when the choices are in order. If it is too big, move to the smaller ones; if too small, the larger ones.
- Back-solving is often faster for word problems about ages, mixtures and money.
## Estimation
Many choices are far apart. A rough estimate can find the answer, or at least remove three choices, in a few seconds.
> What is 49.8% of 6,012? About half of 6,000, so about 3,000.
! Always check how far apart the choices are before calculating precisely. If they are far apart, estimate.
## Calculator dos and don'ts

The on-screen calculator is basic: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, square root and a memory function. It follows the order of operations, but check this in your practice so you are sure.
- Do use it for awkward multiplication or division, such as 37 × 64 or 4,312 ÷ 8.
- Do use it to check a percent change in a data question.
- Do not use it for simple steps you can do in your head. Clicking takes time and invites typing errors.
- Do not use it when the numbers are huge or the question has a pattern; a calculator cannot spot that 2³⁰ − 2²⁹ equals 2²⁹.
- Use the Transfer Display button in numeric entry questions to copy the result straight into the answer box, but check the rounding the question asks for.
## Quantitative Comparison shortcuts
- You are comparing, not calculating. Often you can simplify both quantities the same way: add or subtract the same number from both, or multiply or divide both by the same positive number.
- Never multiply or divide both sides by a quantity that might be negative or zero, because it could reverse or break the comparison.
- If the quantities contain only numbers (no variables), the answer cannot be "cannot be determined". There is always a fixed answer.

- If there are variables, test several kinds of numbers: a positive integer, a negative, zero, a fraction between 0 and 1. If two allowed values give different results, the answer is "cannot be determined".
> Quantity A: x²    Quantity B: x, given x ≠ 0
> x = 2 gives A greater; x = ½ gives B greater. The answer is "cannot be determined".
! Figures are not necessarily drawn to scale. Do not judge an angle or length by how it looks unless the problem gives that information.
## Common traps
- Percent of the wrong base: a rise from 80 to 100 is 25%, but a fall from 100 to 80 is 20%.
- Units: hours versus minutes, thousands versus units, percent versus percentage points.
- "Integer" includes negatives and zero. "Positive" excludes zero.
- Squares: if x² = 25, then x is 5 or −5.
- "Indicate all such values": you must select every correct choice. Check each one.
- Numeric entry: answer exactly what is asked, in the requested units and rounding.
## Data Interpretation
- Before the first question, read the title, labels, units and any notes under the chart.
- Look for the question that can be answered by estimation. Many can.
- Write down the two or three numbers you need before you start any calculation.
## Writing work down
Even when a step feels obvious, write a short note. On a hard question, a written line of work stops you from losing your place, and it makes errors easy to spot when you return in pass 2.
## Practice plan in the app
- Each Quant topic has a lesson with worked examples and a practice set. Start with your weakest topic in the Progress tab.
- After each set, read the explanation for every question, and ask: was there a faster method, such as plugging in or estimation?
- Keep an error log with three causes: concept, calculation or misreading. Most points are lost to the last two, and they are the easiest to fix.

articles.title: Essay tips and a reusable template
lines: The Analytical Writing section is a single "Analyze an Issue" task: you read a short statement and specific instructions, then have 30 minutes to write an essay that takes a position and supports it. You do not need a perfect essay for a good score. You need a clear position, solid reasons with specific examples, logical organization and clean, controlled English.
## What the readers look for
- A clear position that responds to the specific instructions, not just to the general topic.
- Reasons that support the position, developed with concrete examples.
- Awareness of complexity: when the statement might not hold, or what a reasonable opponent would say.
- Logical organization, with clear links between ideas.
- Precise language and varied sentences, with few errors.
! Read the instructions twice. A brilliant essay that ignores what the task asks you to address will lose points. If it asks you to consider when the claim would not hold, you must do that.
## Plan for 3-5 minutes
- Decide your position. A balanced position ("largely true, with an important limit") often gives you more to say than an extreme one.
- Brainstorm three possible reasons, and pick the two or three with the best examples.
- Choose examples from different areas: science, history, business, education, the arts, daily life.
- Note one counterargument and how you will answer it.
## A reusable template
Use this as a framework, not a script. Change the words each time so the essay sounds like you.
> Paragraph 1, introduction (3-4 sentences): Restate the issue in your own words. Say why it matters. State your position, including its limit. Preview your reasons.
> Paragraph 2, first reason: Topic sentence with the reason. A specific example. Two or three sentences explaining how the example supports your position.
> Paragraph 3, second reason: Same structure, with an example from a different area.
> Paragraph 4, the limit or counterargument: Present the strongest opposing view fairly. Explain where it is right and why your position still holds overall.
> Paragraph 5, conclusion (2-3 sentences): Restate your position in new words and say what follows from it.
## A short worked outline
Here is an original practice statement and a plan.
> Statement: "Students learn more from failure than from success."
> Position: Failure teaches more when it is followed by reflection and support; without them, it often teaches only discouragement.
> Reason 1: Failure exposes the exact gap in understanding. Example: a student whose bridge model collapses in an engineering class learns about load in a way a textbook cannot show.
> Reason 2: Success can hide weak methods. Example: a student who memorizes answers passes one test, then struggles in the next course.
> Limit: Repeated failure without feedback can lower motivation. Example: a beginner musician who is only ever corrected, never encouraged, may quit.
> Conclusion: Failure is a powerful teacher, but only when schools design it as a step, not an end.
## Examples that work
- Specific beats general. "A small bakery that switched to online orders during a supply shortage" is better than "many businesses".
- Hypothetical examples are acceptable if they are realistic and clearly explained.
- You do not need famous names or exact dates. Do not invent statistics; an invented number weakens your credibility.
## Language that lifts the score
- Use transitions that show logic: "as a result", "by contrast", "this suggests", "even so".
- Vary sentence length. Mix short, firm sentences with longer ones that join ideas.
- Use precise words, not inflated ones. "Undermines" is better than "is bad for"; "utilize" is not better than "use".
- Avoid repeating the exact wording of the statement in every paragraph.
## Writing and reviewing
- Write the body paragraphs first if the introduction is not coming. You can type it at the top afterwards.
- Aim for four or five paragraphs and roughly 450-650 words. Quality matters more than length, but a very short essay rarely develops its reasons enough.
- Keep 3-5 minutes to reread. Fix missing words, wrong verb forms and unclear sentences. There is no spell checker, so look for typos.
! Keep a short, honest conclusion. A strong final paragraph restates the position and its limit; it does not add a brand-new argument.
## Practice in this app
- Write at least one practice essay a week under the 30-minute timer, typed, with no spell checker.
- After each essay, compare it with the model essay and rate yourself on the 0-6 scale. Be strict: check each point in the list above.
- Keep a list of examples that worked well. Many can be adapted to different statements, especially those about education, technology, leadership and progress.
- In mock tests, the essay comes first, as on the real test. Treat it seriously; it also warms up your focus for the sections that follow.

articles.title: Guessing, marking and reviewing
lines: On the GRE, a wrong answer costs nothing and a blank answer earns nothing. That simple rule shapes three skills that can add several points to your score: guessing well, marking wisely and reviewing efficiently.
## Rule 1: answer every question
Your score counts correct answers only. There is no penalty for a wrong answer. So a guess can only help you. Before any section timer reaches zero, every question should have an answer.
> If you guess randomly on a five-choice question, you have a 20% chance of being right. Remove two wrong choices first and the chance rises to about 33%. Remove three, and it is 50%.
! In the last minute of a section, stop working on any single question. Use the review screen to find unanswered questions and fill them all in.
## Smart guessing in Verbal
- Text Completion: if you can fill one blank with confidence, keep only the choices that fit it and use the clues to pick among the rest of the blanks.
- Sentence Equivalence: you need a pair. Remove any word that has no partner with a similar meaning; often only two or three plausible pairs remain.
- Reading Comprehension: remove extreme choices, choices outside the passage's scope and choices that contradict the main idea. The one that matches the author's general tone is often a good guess.
- Unknown words: decide if a word sounds positive or negative from its roots, and compare that with what the blank needs.
## Smart guessing in Quant
- Estimate. Even a rough sense of size removes choices that are far too big or too small.
- Use the figure carefully. Figures are not necessarily to scale, but if no note says otherwise and you have nothing else, a reasonable reading of the figure is better than a random pick.

- Quantitative Comparison: if the problem has only fixed numbers, "cannot be determined" is wrong, so guess among the other three. If it has variables and you suspect different cases give different results, "cannot be determined" is a sensible guess.
- Numeric entry: enter your best estimate rather than leaving the box empty.
## Marking: when and how
The mark button flags a question so you can find it on the review screen. Use it with a purpose.
- Mark a question when you have guessed but think you could solve it with more time.
- Do not mark a question you have no idea how to solve. Guess, move on and forget it. Marking it only fills your review list with questions you will not get.
- Do not mark questions you are fairly sure about. Second-guessing correct answers is a real risk.
- Aim for no more than three or four marked questions per section, so pass 2 stays short and focused.
## The review screen
At any time inside a section you can open the review screen. It shows each question, whether it is answered and whether it is marked. Click a question to go straight to it.
- Use it at your planned checkpoint, or when you finish pass 1.
- First look for any question marked "not answered" and answer it.
- Then work through marked questions, starting with the one you felt closest to solving.
## Changing answers
- Change an answer when you find a clear reason: you misread the question, made a calculation error or found the clue you missed.
- Do not change an answer just because it "feels wrong" on a second look. Your first careful answer is usually better than an anxious second guess.
- If you change an answer in Quant, redo the key step, not the whole problem.
## Reviewing questions you answered
If you finish a section early, review in this order:
- Quant: numeric entry answers (units, rounding, decimal point), then "select all" questions, then questions with negative numbers or percents.
- Verbal: Text Completion with several blanks (reread the full passage with your answers), then select-one-or-more reading questions.
## After the test: review your practice
Guessing and marking are skills, and you improve them with practice. After each mock test in this app:
- Count how many of your marked questions you got right in pass 2. If it is low, you are marking the wrong questions.
- Count how many questions you changed, and whether the changes helped. If changes often hurt, trust your first answer more.
- Look at the questions you guessed on. Are they all from one topic? That topic should go to the top of next week's plan, and the Progress tab will show it among your weak topics.

articles.title: Test anxiety and stamina
lines: Almost everyone feels nervous about the GRE. A little nervousness helps you focus. Too much makes you read the same sentence three times, forget a formula you know well or rush through easy questions. The good news is that both anxiety and stamina respond to training, just like vocabulary or algebra.
## Why the test feels stressful
- It is timed, and the timer is visible.
- It matters for goals you care about.
- It adapts, so a hard section can feel like failure even when it means you did well.
- There is no scheduled break, so nearly two hours of focus are needed.
Knowing these reasons helps. When you notice the pressure, you can name it: "This is the timer stress I expected." Naming a feeling often reduces it.
## Familiarity is the best cure
Uncertainty feeds anxiety. Remove as much of it as you can before test day.
- Know the exact format, order and timing of every section. Read the format article until it feels boring.
- Take full mock tests in realistic conditions: same time of day, phone away, no pauses, essay included.
- Practice the check-in steps for at-home testing, or visit the route to your test center.
- Decide your pacing plan and checkpoints in advance, so you do not make decisions under pressure.
## A breathing reset
Use this when your mind races or you notice your shoulders are tense. It takes about 20 seconds.
> Breathe in slowly through your nose for a count of four.
> Hold for a count of two.
> Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of six.
> Repeat twice, then reread the question from the start.
Practice it during mock tests so it is automatic on the day.
## Thoughts that help
- "One question is worth very little. I can let this one go."
- "Hard questions mean I am probably doing well."
- "I have practiced this. I know what to do next."
- "Mark, guess, move on."

Thoughts that hurt are often predictions: "I am going to fail", "Everyone else finds this easy". When you notice one, return your attention to the task in front of you: the next sentence, the next number.
! Do not try to calculate your score during the test. It takes attention away from the questions and is almost always wrong.
## Building stamina
The GRE asks for close to two hours of concentration without a break. Stamina is built gradually.
- Weeks 1-2 of your plan: study in focused blocks of 30-45 minutes.
- Middle weeks: extend to blocks of 60-75 minutes, such as two sections back to back.
- Final weeks: take full mock tests, about 2 hours, at least once a week.
- Train on paper or screen the same way you will test, including your note-taking material.
## The body matters
- Sleep: keep a regular sleep time for the last two weeks. One late night of revision does more harm than good.
- Food: eat a normal meal one to two hours before the test. Avoid trying a new food or drink that day.
- Caffeine: if you usually drink coffee or tea, have your normal amount; do not double it.
- Movement: a short walk before the test can lower tension.
## During the test
- Between sections, sit back, breathe slowly once and drop your shoulders.
- If you feel your focus slipping in a long passage, read one sentence at a time and summarize it in a few words.
- If you blank on a formula, write down what you do know. Often the rest comes back.
- If one section goes badly, treat the next one as a fresh start. Sections are scored separately.
## When anxiety is very strong

If test anxiety often stops you from working, even in practice, talk to someone you trust, a teacher or a counselor. Support is a normal part of preparing for an important exam. If you have a documented condition, ETS offers testing accommodations; read the details and the request process on ets.org early, because it can take time.
## Using the app for confidence
- Start with practice sets on your strongest topic to build momentum, then move to a weak one.
- Watch your Progress tab. Seeing accuracy rise week by week is real evidence that you are improving.
- Take your mocks seriously but kindly. A low score in week 2 is information, not a verdict.
- Before the real test, look back at your first mock result. You have already come a long way.

articles.title: A 4-week study plan
lines: Four weeks is a short runway. It works best if you already have a fair base in English and high-school math and need to sharpen skills, learn the format and build pacing. Plan on about 2 hours a day on weekdays and 3-4 hours on one weekend day, which adds up to roughly 55 hours.
## Principles for a short plan
- Find your weak topics fast, then spend most of your time on them.
- Learn the format and pacing early; they are quick wins.
- Do vocabulary every day in short sessions, not in big blocks.
- Take a full mock test every weekend.
! With only four weeks, do not try to cover every topic equally. Points come fastest from weak topics that appear often, such as Text Completion, reading and core algebra.
## Before you start (day 1)
- Read the guide articles in "The exam" group: format, question types and scoring.
- Take Mock Test 1 under real conditions, essay included. This is your baseline.
- Open the Progress tab and write down your five weakest topics, plus your estimated Verbal and Quant scores.
## Week 1: foundations and diagnosis
- Daily: 15 minutes of vocabulary flashcards (about 20 new words, plus review).
- Verbal: lessons and practice sets for Text Completion and Sentence Equivalence.
- Quant: lessons and practice sets for number properties, arithmetic and percents, and the two weakest Quant topics from your mock.
- Read the strategy articles on time management and on guessing and marking.
- Write one practice essay under the 30-minute timer and rate it against the model essay.
- Weekend: take Mock Test 2. Compare section 1 accuracy with Mock Test 1.
## Week 2: weak topics
- Daily: vocabulary flashcards, now reviewing missed words first.
- Verbal: reading comprehension lessons and practice sets (short passages, long passages, arguments).
- Quant: algebra and word problems, then your next weakest Quant topic from the Progress tab.
- Redo any practice set where you scored below 70%, after rereading its lesson.
- Read the Verbal tips and Quant tips articles and try one technique on each set (prediction in Verbal, plugging in or back-solving in Quant).
- Write one practice essay and use the template from the essay article.
- Weekend: take Mock Test 3. Review every wrong answer and every guessed answer.
## Week 3: pressure and mixed practice
- Daily: vocabulary flashcards.
- Practice sets with the timer for every topic still marked weak.
- Quant: geometry and data interpretation lessons and practice sets, if not already done.
- Mixed review: one Verbal and one Quant practice set from different topics every day, to practice switching.
- Write one practice essay.
- Midweek: take Mock Test 4 under real conditions.
- Weekend: take Mock Test 5. Use the checkpoints from the time management article.
## Week 4: polish and rest
- Days 1-3: return to the two topics where your accuracy is still lowest. Redo their practice sets and reread their lessons.
- Day 3 or 4: take Mock Test 6 at the same time of day as your real test. This is your last full mock.
- Days 5-6: light review only: flashcards, a few explanations from earlier mocks, the essay template.
- Read the test day and test anxiety articles. Prepare your ID, route or room.
- Day before the test: no new material. A short walk, an early night.
## How to know you are on track
- Your section 1 accuracy rises from mock to mock.
- You finish every section with every question answered.
- The weak-topic list in the Progress tab gets shorter or changes.

If after Mock Test 4 your estimates are still far below your goal, consider whether a longer plan and a later test date would serve you better. The 8-week plan builds the same skills with more time for practice.

articles.title: An 8-week study plan
lines: Eight weeks is a comfortable length for most test takers. It gives you time to learn every topic once, practice your weak areas properly and build stamina with regular full mocks. Plan on about 1.5 hours on weekdays and 3 hours on one weekend day, roughly 80-90 hours in total.
## Principles
- Two phases: weeks 1-4 build skills topic by topic; weeks 5-8 turn them into test performance.
- Vocabulary every day, 15-20 minutes.
- One full mock test every week or two, more often near the end.
- One timed essay every week.
! Keep a short error log from the first week: question, topic, why you missed it (concept, careless, timing, vocabulary). It will guide every later week.
## Before you start
- Read the articles in "The exam" group.
- Take Mock Test 1 as a baseline, essay included.
- Note your estimated scores and the five weakest topics from the Progress tab.
## Week 1: number basics and Text Completion
- Quant: lessons and practice sets on number properties, fractions and decimals, and percents.
- Verbal: Text Completion lessons and practice sets (one, two and three blanks).
- Vocabulary: about 20 new flashcards a day, plus review.
- Essay: read the essay article; write one practice essay without a timer to learn the template.
## Week 2: algebra and Sentence Equivalence
- Quant: lessons and practice sets on linear equations, inequalities and exponents.
- Verbal: Sentence Equivalence lessons and practice sets.
- Read the time management article and start timing every practice set.
- Essay: one timed essay; rate it against the model essay.
- Weekend: take Mock Test 2.
## Week 3: word problems and reading
- Quant: word problems (rates, work, mixtures, ratios) and any algebra topic below 70%.
- Verbal: Reading Comprehension lessons and practice sets on short passages.
- Read the Quant tips article and practice plugging in and back-solving.
- Essay: one timed essay.
## Week 4: geometry, data and long reading
- Quant: geometry lessons and practice sets; data interpretation lessons and practice sets.
- Verbal: long passages and argument paragraphs.
- Read the Verbal tips article.
- Weekend: take Mock Test 3. Compare with Mock Test 1 topic by topic.
## Week 5: weak topics, round 1
- Pick the four weakest topics from the Progress tab and your error log.
- For each: reread the lesson, redo the practice set, read every explanation.
- Statistics and counting topics if not yet covered.
- Read the guessing and marking article; practice the two-pass method on every set.
- Essay: one timed essay.
- Weekend: take Mock Test 4.
## Week 6: mixed timed practice
- Mixed daily sets: one Verbal, one Quant, from different topics.
- Focus on section 1 accuracy: in each mock, review every section 1 error first.
- Essay: one timed essay, written in a new area (science, education, business) each time.
- Midweek: Mock Test 5. Weekend: Mock Test 6.
## Week 7: weak topics, round 2 and stamina
- Return to the topics that are still weak. If one has improved, replace it with the next one on the list.
- Read the test anxiety and stamina article and practice the breathing reset in mocks.
- Essay: one timed essay.
- Midweek: Mock Test 7. Weekend: Mock Test 8, at the same time of day as your real test.
## Week 8: final polish
- Days 1-3: reread your error log. Redo the five questions in it that taught you the most.
- Day 3: Mock Test 9, your last full mock.
- Days 4-6: light work only: flashcards, the essay template, a few explanations.
- Read the test day article and prepare your ID and route or room.
- Day before the test: rest. No new material.
## Checking progress
- After weeks 2, 4 and 6, compare your mock estimates and section 1 accuracy.
- If one measure is moving slowly, shift 30 minutes a day from the stronger measure to it.
- If you are ahead of your goal by week 6, use the extra time for harder sets in your strongest topics, to push section 2 into the harder level.

articles.title: A 12-week study plan
lines: Twelve weeks suits you if you are aiming for a big score increase, have been away from math for a while, are building academic English vocabulary, or can only study about an hour a day. The plan moves slowly through the basics, then adds speed and full-length practice. Plan on 1 hour on weekdays and 2-3 hours on one weekend day, roughly 90-100 hours in total.
## Three phases
- Weeks 1-5, foundations: learn every topic with its lesson and practice set.
- Weeks 6-9, strengthening: timed practice, weak topics, regular mocks.
- Weeks 10-12, test readiness: full mocks, stamina, final polish.
! Consistency beats intensity. An hour every day for twelve weeks does far more than three long weekends of cramming.
## Before you start
- Read the articles in "The exam" group so you know the format and scoring.
- Take Mock Test 1 as a baseline, essay included. Do not worry about the score; it is a starting point.
- Set a daily vocabulary goal: about 15 new flashcards a day, which covers the full deck with time for review.
## Week 1: numbers and the logic of Text Completion
- Quant: integers and number properties lesson and practice set.
- Verbal: Text Completion with one blank.
- Read the question types tour article.
## Week 2: fractions, percents and two- and three-blank completions
- Quant: fractions, decimals, percents and ratios.
- Verbal: Text Completion with two and three blanks.
- Essay: read the essay article and write one untimed essay with the template.
## Week 3: exponents and Sentence Equivalence
- Quant: exponents, roots and absolute value.
- Verbal: Sentence Equivalence.
- Redo any practice set from weeks 1-2 that scored below 70%.
## Week 4: algebra and short reading
- Quant: equations and inequalities.
- Verbal: short reading passages.
- Essay: one timed essay; rate it against the model essay.
- Weekend: Mock Test 2.
## Week 5: functions, word problems and long reading
- Quant: functions, quadratics and coordinate geometry; word problems.
- Verbal: long reading passages and argument paragraphs.
- Read the Verbal tips and Quant tips articles.
## Week 6: geometry
- Quant: lines, angles, triangles and polygons; circles, solids and coordinate figures.
- Verbal: one mixed timed practice set every other day.
- Read the time management article and start timing every set.
- Essay: one timed essay.
## Week 7: data, statistics and counting
- Quant: statistics; counting, probability and sets; data interpretation.
- Verbal: redo the two weakest Verbal sets.
- Weekend: Mock Test 3. Compare your topic accuracy with Mock Test 1.
## Week 8: weak topics, round 1
- Take the five weakest topics from the Progress tab. For each: reread the lesson, redo the set, read every explanation.
- Read the guessing and marking article and use the two-pass method in every set.
- Essay: one timed essay.
- Weekend: Mock Test 4.
## Week 9: mixed timed practice
- Daily: one Verbal and one Quant set from different topics, timed.
- Start an error log if you have not already: topic, reason for the error, what to do next time.
- Weekend: Mock Test 5.
## Week 10: stamina
- Two full mocks this week: Mock Tests 6 and 7, at the time of day of your real test.
- Read the test anxiety and stamina article and practice the breathing reset.
- Between mocks, review every wrong answer and every guess.
- Essay: covered inside the mocks.
## Week 11: weak topics, round 2
- Return to the topics still marked weak. Redo sets until you score 80% or higher.
- Mock Test 8 midweek, Mock Test 9 at the weekend.
- Review your vocabulary misses; most of the deck should now feel familiar.
## Week 12: final polish
- Days 1-2: reread your error log and the essay template.
- Day 3: Mock Test 10, your last full mock.
- Days 4-6: light review only. Read the test day article and prepare your ID and route or room.
- Day before the test: rest.
## Keep the plan flexible
- If a topic clicks quickly, move on early and bank the time for a harder one.
- If you fall behind by a week, drop one mock from weeks 10-11 rather than skipping lessons.
- After about ten mocks you still have more in the app; use them for a retake plan if you need one.

articles.title: How to use your mock results
lines: A mock test is worth far more after you finish it than while you are taking it. The score is only the headline. The real value is in the details: which questions you missed, why you missed them and what that says about the next week of study. Plan to spend at least as long reviewing a mock as taking it.
## Step 1: read the scores in context
- Note your estimated Verbal and Quant scores and your essay self-rating.
- Look at section 1 accuracy for each measure. It decides which level of section 2 you receive, so it is the most useful single number.
- Note which level of section 2 you reached: easier, medium or harder.
! One mock score is noisy. Look for the trend across three or more mocks before you change your plan in a big way.
## Step 2: review every question you missed
For each wrong answer, read the explanation and classify the error. Use four labels.
- Concept: you did not know the rule, word or method.
- Careless: you knew it but slipped: a sign error, misread number, wrong blank.
- Timing: you rushed it, or guessed because time ran out.
- Trap: you chose an answer that looked right for a reason the explanation describes.
> Example log line: Quant S1 Q7, percents, careless: used 100 as the base instead of 80. Fix: write "base =" before every percent change.
## Step 3: review your guesses and slow questions

Questions you got right by luck are hidden weaknesses. Review every question you guessed on, and every question that took more than about 3 minutes, even if you got it right. Ask whether a faster method existed.
## Step 4: find the pattern
After the review, count your labels.
- Mostly concept errors: go back to lessons and practice sets for those topics.
- Mostly careless errors: slow down slightly in section 1, write more steps and check numeric entry answers.
- Mostly timing errors: use the target times and checkpoints from the time management article, and practice mark and move.
- Mostly trap errors: study the explanations for the trap types. In Verbal, they often involve extreme or out-of-scope answers; in Quant, wrong bases and untested cases.
## Step 5: update your plan
- Open the Progress tab. It ranks your weak topics using all your practice and mock answers.
- Choose the top two or three for the coming week.
- For each: reread the lesson, redo the practice set, and read every explanation.
- Add any missed vocabulary words to your daily flashcard review.
## Using the essay self-rating
- Compare your essay with the model essay paragraph by paragraph.
- Did you follow the specific instructions? Is your position clear in the first paragraph?
- Are your examples specific? Is there a paragraph that deals with a counterargument or limit?
- Rate yourself honestly on the 0-6 scale, and note one thing to change in the next essay.
## How often to take mocks
- Early in your plan: every one to two weeks, to measure progress without using up the mocks too fast.
- Final three weeks: one or two a week, to build stamina and pacing.
- Leave four to six days between your last mock and the real test.
## What progress looks like
- Section 1 accuracy rising across mocks, and more frequent harder section 2 levels.
- Fewer careless and timing errors, even if concept errors remain on new topics.
- The weak-topic list in the Progress tab changing as old weaknesses improve.
- Finishing every section with all questions answered and a minute or two for review.
## A note on score estimates

The app's 130-170 estimates follow the real test's two-stage design and are based on your total correct answers and your section 2 level. They are a guide to your current level, not a promise of your official score. Your real score can be a little higher or lower on the day. If your last three mock estimates are steady and close to your goal, you are ready to book or sit the test.
